newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Army rampages in Zaire town, no sign of refugees.
newsitem.headline: Army rampages in Zaire town, no sign of refugees.

text.p: Drunk or ill-disciplined soldiers who drifted west after their defeat by Tutsi rebels in east Zaire subjected the town of Kisangani to a second night of shooting and looting, witnesses said on Sunday.

But Roman Catholic church workers and local businessmen who are keen to help displaced Zaireans and refugees fleeing the Tutsi revolt in the east said a charter flight over the region had found no evidence of a major exodus.

"A pilot who flew over Lubutu and Walikale this morning saw a few groups on the road. That was all," one Roman Catholic missionary told Reuters on Saturday. "It may be that they are taking forest paths but we may be talking of only a few thousands instead of many thousands."
The Kisangani Chamber of Commerce and the Roman Catholic Church are trying to locate and help the refugees.
"We are organising a convoy to bring back the sick and supply what we can on the ground," Raymond Mokeni, chairman of the Chamber of Commerce, told Reuters.

"Because of the insecurity along the road both the displaced and local villagers spend the day in the forest and only return to the road at night," he said. "If we can supply them there, they won't have to come to Kisangani."

Kisangani is the last outpost of tenuous Zairean authority before tens of thousands of square kilometres (miles) of forest and hills in which an unknown number of Hutu refugees from Rwanda or Burundi and displaced Zaireans are hiding.
Kisangani governor Lombeya Bosongo said the authorities were aware of the problem. "We are looking at the possibility of refugees arriving but it is not a preoccupation."

Heavy overnight gunfire rocked the town on Friday night and at least three businesses were looted. "The tension here is too much. I will have to get my family out," one businessman said, as troops continued to trickle in from the war front.
Soldiers cruise the usually quiet streets in vehicles commandeered from aid workers before the retreat.
Calm returned on Saturday and shops reopened, but fresh shooting and looting took place on Saturday night.
An unconfirmed report said one soldier had been shot dead on Friday night by troops seeking to restore order. There were no other immediate reports of casualties.

Kisangani, about 500 km (325 miles) from the conflict zone, is a likely staging post for any relief operation for Hutu refugees who are believed to have trekked west to escape the fighting and the danger of reprisals from rival Tutsis.
Foreign aid workers pulled out of eastern Zaire over a week ago as insecurity spread to the huge refugee camps of Goma and Bukavu.

The whereabouts of many of the 1.2 million Hutu refugees from the camps remains a mystery but reports filtering out of eastern Zaire talk of refugees dying from thirst and exhaustion in the granite hills. Aid groups fear epidemics of cholera and dysentery.
The Hutus fled Rwanda in 1994 fearing reprisals after Hutu hardliners massacred hundreds of thousands of Tutsis. Zaire says Tutsi-led Rwanda is behind the revolt in the east.

Meanwhile, 11 tonnes of aid from Spain -- food, blankets and tents -- arrived in the Zairean capital Kinshasa on Sunday. Officials said it would be given to the national Red Cross for distribution to displaced Zaireans, possibly from Kisangani.
